doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Groovin' High versus a two-chord vamp
summary: Ries compares playing a jazz standard with the supportive role in Miss You.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. That’s an astute player required for that kind of thing I think. And your solos, like that particular solo that’s probably like a one chord vamp?
Right. That was two chords, but yeah.
Yeah. Is that harder or easier, or is it both? I mean if you were playing “Groovin’ High” and then you play, over here you’ve got a two chord vamp, which is more challenging?

You know they both have their challenges, not challenges but I don’t want to say limitations, they both have their differences in the sense that with “Groovin’ High” I’m just playing with a jazz group and I can kind of — do I defer to Dizzy and Bird, thinking about that, or do I just try to do my thing on that song? But I’m still trying to do my thing also on “Miss You” because the original song with Bobby Keys I’m not playing like Bobby but I don’t want to be too far from it because I’m riffing, and again I’m playing because Mick is out there in front of the people so the show is about supporting the Stones as best I can and so I’m in a supportive role in that way and then with “Groovin’ High” I’m I guess freer in a sense because I’m not worrying about so much okay this person is coming in singing the verse so maybe it’s slightly freer that way.
But there’s more chord — there’s a chord progression to pay more attention to.
Oh yeah, that’s true, of course, yeah. Yeah and then it’s like in these chords in this way how do I want to — how far do I want to take this.
